# How This Book Differs {#sec-different .unnumbered}

There is a lot of free Google Earth Engine material on the internet. Some of it is excellent. Before asking anyone to spend time here, it is worth being precise about what this book does that the free material does not, and honest about what the free material does better.

## What is already out there, and where it stops

The official Earth Engine guides are accurate, current and written by the people who built the platform. They are reference documentation. They tell you what `reduceRegion` does. They do not tell you that the `scale` argument you pass to it is a scientific decision that will change your reported mangrove area by four percent, or that reporting the area without the scale makes the number unusable.

Course material from the major providers is well structured and usually free. It is also built around clean demonstration areas, typically somewhere with reliable clear skies, and it stops at the point where the map appears. The step that follows, deciding whether the map is good enough to put a name on, is the step the work actually consists of.

Video tutorials get you to a result fastest of anything on the list. They are also the least recoverable when something breaks, because you watched a decision being made rather than reading why it was made.

And the pattern common to nearly all of it: code first, physics never. You are shown how to compute NDVI in the second minute and never told why the near infrared plateau exists, so when NDVI saturates over dense canopy and stops responding, there is nothing to reason from.

## What six years produced

This book comes out of six years of doing this work and teaching it, in forestry, coastal conservation, precision agriculture and commercial site selection. The material has been through a five week industry bootcamp, a three day GeoAI intensive for conservation practitioners, university teaching, and delivery work where a wrong map had a consequence.

Four things came out of that which are hard to get from a tutorial.

**The failures are documented, not just the successes.** A tutorial shows the path that worked. This book shows the mangrove classification that put forest on a hillside because elevation was left out of the stack, the composite that was full of cloud because it used a QA band that stopped being populated in 2022, and the model that reported perfect accuracy because a predictor variable was a disguised copy of the target. Every one of those is a real error from real work, and each is now a named failure mode you can recognise before it costs you a week.

**The physics comes first, because the debugging depends on it.** The book opens with ten Principles chapters on how sensors see and where the field is heading (their only code is the short Python that draws their figures, and P10 teaches a point-and-click app), and Part I has no code at all. That is deliberate and it is the single biggest structural difference between this book and the free material. When a classifier confuses mangrove with oil palm, the fix is not a better classifier. The fix is knowing that both are dense broadleaf canopy with nearly identical spectral signatures, and that what separates them is texture, elevation and radar structure. That reasoning is unavailable to someone who learned the API but not the instrument.

**The tropical case is the default case, not the exception.** Most teaching material assumes you can find a clear scene. Across equatorial Indonesia, the Congo basin and much of the Amazon, you frequently cannot, in any given year. Cloud masking is treated here as a prerequisite rather than an optional refinement, radar arrives early rather than as an advanced topic, and every worked example runs over places where the sky is genuinely a problem.

**The chain runs all the way to the decision.** Free material generally ends at the classified map. Here the chain continues: accuracy assessment that would survive review, area estimates with the scale stated, and then the applications that pay for the work, whether that is a blue carbon MRV submission, a national FOLU Net Sink commitment, or a site selection score a business will act on. A map that nobody can act on is a hobby.

## What the free material does better

Currency. The official documentation is updated the day a feature ships; a book is a snapshot. Where a dataset identifier or an API signature has changed since publication, the documentation is right and this book is wrong. Check it.

Breadth of dataset coverage. The Earth Engine catalogue holds hundreds of collections. This book uses a few dozen, chosen because they carry the teaching: Landsat, Sentinel-1 and -2, GEDI, GRACE, CHIRPS, the Hansen and tropical moist forest change maps, WorldCover and a handful more. If you need atmospheric chemistry, ocean colour or anything the chapters do not touch, the catalogue documentation is where to go.

Community answers. When you hit an error message nobody anticipated, the Earth Engine developers forum and Stack Exchange will usually have it. Appendix B covers the errors that recur; it does not attempt to cover all of them.

Use all three alongside this book. They are complementary, not competing.

## What changed, and what did not

Six years is long enough in this field to have watched a methodology become obsolete. It is worth being explicit about which parts of this book are permanent and which are current.

**Slow to change, and refined rather than replaced.** Physics does update, but slowly, and mostly by refinement: better measurements sharpen the constants, better models describe the canopy and the atmosphere more closely, and this book follows the current theory and says so where it matters. What does not turn over is the core. Chlorophyll will keep absorbing red light and leaf mesophyll will keep scattering near infrared. Water will keep absorbing in the shortwave. Mangroves will keep growing in the intertidal band. Every technique built on those facts, band ratios, spectral separability reasoning, the ecological logic behind adding elevation to a feature stack, works as well today as it did in 2019 and will work in 2035, improved at the edges as the theory improves. The Principles and Part I are the parts of this book that age most slowly.

**Changed completely.** In 2019 the accepted workflow was to hand build a feature stack, spectral bands, indices, texture, radar, terrain, then feed it two thousand carefully collected training points. That was the state of the art and this book teaches it in full, in Parts III to V, because it remains the method you fall back on when nothing else fits and because it is the only way to understand what the newer approach automated away. Since 2024, Google's satellite embeddings compress spectral, spatial and multi sensor context into 64 learned dimensions per pixel, and a comparable map can be trained from twenty points, with no compositing and no feature engineering. Chapter [-@sec-embeddings] does the whole thing again this way, over the same area, so you can compare the two maps side by side.

**Changed direction, not just degree.** Analysis used to be retrospective: map what happened. Increasing predictive capacity moved the useful question forward in time, from where was forest lost to where is forest likely to be lost next. That changes what conservation resources are for, and Chapters [-@sec-timeseries] and [-@sec-vector] treat prediction as a first class output rather than a footnote.

**Why the old way is still taught here.** Because the new tools fail in ways only the old understanding can diagnose. Embeddings are annual, so they cannot answer a question about a single storm. They are opaque, so when a boundary looks wrong there is no band to inspect. They depend on Google's release schedule. Someone who only ever learned the embedding shortcut has no way to check whether the shortcut worked. Someone who learned both can pick.

## What this book will not do for you

Three limits are worth stating plainly, because each one is a place where a reader could expect more than the book gives.

It is a working foundation, not a degree. The physics in the Principles and Part I is enough to reason with when a map looks wrong; it does not replace a course in it, and it will not make anyone a remote sensing scientist in a weekend.

It stays inside the toolbox it teaches. Earth Engine, Python and R are used for data preparation, classical machine learning and statistics. Deep learning appears once, as a small U-Net trained on a Colab GPU in Chapter [-@sec-deeplearning] and compared honestly with a random forest; designing new network architectures, and running them in production, is beyond this book.

It cannot give you field data. Every chapter validates against the best reference it can find (field plots, published inventories, official statistics, other agencies' maps) and says plainly when that reference is weak. Real ground truth is still collected by boat, on foot, in mud. That work has no shortcut, and any tool that claims otherwise is selling something.
